thread.title: Where Are We? CAPE Cod, CAPE Horn Or CAPE Of Good Hope?

author: The Fortune Teller
title: Where Are We? CAPE Cod, CAPE Horn Or CAPE Of Good Hope?
text:
Background With less than half of 2018 ahead of us, both the S&P 500 ( SPY ) and Nasdaq 100 ( QQQ ) are on pace for a record 10th straight up year.
However, before reaching the 10th anniversary since the subprime crisis, it's important to take a closer look at few aspects. After all, you don't want to renew vows (with the market) just before the market decides that the terms and conditions that led into 2009 are no longer relevant when we get closer to 2019.
Dictionary CAPE (Cyclically Adjusted Price to Earnings) ratio: Price earnings ratio based on average inflation-adjusted earnings from the previous 10 years, known as the Cyclically Adjusted PE Ratio (CAPE Ratio), Shiller PE Ratio, or PE 10
Cape Cod is a hook-shaped peninsula of the US state of Massachusetts and a popular summertime destination.
Cod is a large marine fish with a small barbel on the chin.
For the sake of this article the Cod represents a neutral, peaceful environment that may turn stormy, i.e. the type of CAPE we can live with... for now...
Cape Horn is a rocky headland on Hornos Island, in southern Chile's Tierra del Fuego archipelago.
Horn is (among other things) a device sounding a warning or other signal.
For the sake of this article, the horn represents a pessimistic, noisy and nervous environment, i.e. the type of CAPE we have nothing to worry about.
The Cape of Good Hope is a rocky headland on the Atlantic coast of the Cape Peninsula, South Africa.
Good hope is, well, just as it sounds - good hope...
For the sake of this article, the good hope represents an optimistic, good and hopeful environment filled with good hope, i.e. the type of CAPE we should worry about.
This is not a geography lesson. Instead, this is an attempt to see where are we from a CAPE-related perspective and to determine is this environment is i) neutral, quiet and peaceful, ii) pessimistic, noisy and nervous, or iii) an optimistic, good and hopeful market for investors.
Yield Curve The yield curve continues to be one of the most closely-watched gauge - and rightly so. An inverted yield curve has been a very reliable indicator over many decades and it would be foolish to ignore the signal it sends.
In regard to the yield curve it is interesting to note two things:
1. The short-end of the yield curve is reaching new highs almost daily/weekly. The yields on 1-month, 3-month, 6-month, and 1-year Treasury debts ended the week at their highest levels in 10 years!
1-Month LIBOR based on US Dollar data by YCharts
2. With the 10-5 at 0.10% and 10-2 at 0.29%, spreads are as tighter as they were in 11 years!
10-Year Treasury Rate data by YCharts
Central Banks' Balance Sheets, Markets And FAANG We already touched upon this a month ago. Still, it seems that many investors don't pay enough attention to the high correlation between the central banks' balance sheets and the capital markets.
Over the past two weeks before June ended, the aggregate balance sheet of the three largest CBs shrank. The Fed tightened ~$29B, the BoJ tightened ~$34B and only the ECB increased its balance sheet by ~€15B.
Now, that a new month has started, the CBs' balance sheets are inflating again. The result? Trade wars become a non-issue...
SPY Price data by YCharts
Last week I wrote about the FAANG gang : Facebook ( FB ), Apple ( AAPL ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Netflix ( NFLX ), and Alphabet's Google (NASDAQ: GOOG ) ( GOOGL ). As I expected, the article wasn't welcomed by most readers.
Thing is that the FAANG is also (and perhaps even more) correlated to CB's balance sheet than the main indices. Look for yourself:
Perhaps it's time to remind you what no other than Goldman Sachs ( GS ) CEO Lloyd Blankfein said less than three months ago during a CNBC interview:
What didn’t feel standard were the conditions over the last couple of years. People will debate back and forth what’s normal what’s the new normal but conditions where interest rates are zero, yield curves are flat, there's no risk premium. Where central banks all around the world are buying all the risky assets which then therefore put a damper on volatility and the opportunities to perform, that’s not a natural state.
We have not reversed all of that, but we’re walking that back and walking to so the first indications of a withdrawal from what is an unnatural state. The market becomes a bit more volatile, people get compensated for the risk that they're taking. Our clients are doing better consequently we’re doing better with them. So I wouldn’t say we’re popping champagne corks. But we can certainly see what happens when we start to walk back towards a normal financial market.
Unsurprisingly, the peak in the markets in late January 2018 occurred just as CBs' balance sheets peaked. Anyone underestimating the power and contribution of CBs to what we've seen over the past decade - across the board - is making a big mistake.
Although it's certainly not "mission impossible" for stocks to reach new record highs, it's hard(er) to expect the markets to overcome the previous peaks without new money being injected into the systems; just as it was until not too long ago.
The thing is that the exact opposite is happening. The Fed QT plan is now reaching the fourth (four of five) stage. In this stage, the monthly reductions are expected to be $40B/month.
The target for October remains very ambitiously low.
While the Fed is stepping up its balance sheet reduction, the ECB is actually expected to do the exact opposite. On top of the routine €30B purchases, there is going to be another €18B of new-additional investments as a result of maturing debts.
Overall, this may be a good month for stocks to try and push higher. Not only that the end of the month is traditionally the time when the Fed reduces the most but such months - where the ECB is pouring circa €50B to the markets - are rare and expected to end soon, per the ECB's own schedule.
August, specifically looks like a potentially rough month. The Fed will shed another $40B and the ECB's reinvesting amount is going to be tiny. With the aggregate CB's balance sheets moving down by that much, August might turn out into a problematic month.
CAPE The current Shiller P/E ratio is 32.80
Is it high, low, medium? Let's just say that the stats looks like this:
Mean: 16.85 Median: 16.15 Min: 4.78 (Dec 1920) Max: 44.19 (Dec 1999) In case that the CAPE at 32.80 doesn't seem to you as high; here's a more in-depth dive into the data around it:
No matter how you turn/twist things around, the current CAPE is high/expensive.
Volatility The VIX ( VXX ) continues to trade at very low levels. Nonetheless, GS reminds us that July is the best month to go long volatility.
Taking into consideration that Credit Suisse ( CS ) Global Risk Appetite measure is signaling "Panic" these days - buying volatility may not be such a bad idea...
More than anything, it's the below chart that caught my eyes. This chart is combining volatility with the yield curve. Basically, what you can see is that lower 10-2 spread is quite a good indication for what is going to happen with volatility about 30 months later...
The question now is, therefore, which half of the glass do we look at. The half full shows that we may have at least another 30 months of bull market ahead of us. The half empty shows that we may have another 30 months of bull market ahead of us at best ; that's especially true taking into consideration that during the collapse of the 10-2 spread since 2014 hasn't been accompanied by any move up by the VIX whatsoever.
Putting it differently, the VIX is lagging the 30-month 10-2 early indicator by about 2 years already; when will it catch up?...
Debt Debt levels are soaring, reaching levels that we had seen before the subprime crisis.
Here's another, perhaps even more colorful way to put it:
Many dismiss debt as something that can be rolled over and over again, just as can may be kicked down the road. However, if you go back to what we've started this article with - rising rates/yields, especially the short-end of the curve, you'll realize that debt is soaring at a very bad timing.
Credit spreads have widened significantly over the past 5+ months and refinancing is not as easy as it used to be.
US Corporate Master Option-Adjusted Spread data by YCharts
Bottom Line As far as I'm concerned, we're neither at cape cod nor at the cape of good hope. Does this leave us with cape horn? I'll leave it for you to decide which type of CAPE you believe we're at. Feel free to express your own CAPE view (cod, horn or good hope) through the comment section.
Just as I wrote a few days ago: Opportunity Or Threat? It All Lies In The Eyes Of The Beholder And The Portfolio Of The Holder ; the same applies to your own-personal CAPE assessment I guess.
Nevertheless, when it comes to obvious issues - it's not recommended to have your head in the clouds (not paying much attention to what is happening around you) or to bury your head in the sand (refuse to think about unpleasant facts, although they will have an influence on your situation), voluntarily.
Because between these Talking Heads , the last thing you wish your portfolio to turn into is a Psycho Killer ... (of wealth)
